claims.text: High-temperature oxidizing exposure induces preferential Mg segregation at defects and phase interfaces in non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Corrosive exposure induces preferential Mg segregation at defects and phase interfaces in these alloys.
Preferential Mg segregation drives the transformation of metastable solid solutions into stable intermetallic compounds.
Phase evolution changes local chemistry and electrochemical potential.
Phase evolution modifies the protective oxide scale.
The initial alloy has an overall density below 6 g/cm³.
The initial alloy contains heterogeneous metastable solid-solution regions and dispersed intermetallic precipitates.
An untreated as-cast sample set can serve as the controlled baseline for environmentally aged samples.
Oxidation at approximately 800 °C is an example of the proposed accelerated environmental-aging treatment.
The proposed elevated-temperature oxidizing and chloride-containing environments are known to promote Mg mobility.
Mg accumulation at grain boundaries or interphase interfaces facilitates nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic compounds.
Mg segregation lowers local activation barriers for transformation of metastable solid solutions.
Changes in local alloy composition can affect oxide-scale adhesion, morphology, and oxidation resistance.
Environmentally treated samples will have a larger stable-intermetallic phase fraction than the untreated baseline.
Environmentally treated samples will show a measurable corrosion-potential shift relative to the untreated baseline.
Environmentally treated samples will exhibit altered oxide-scale thickness, spallation behavior, or phase composition.
The hypothesis is restricted to density-below-6 g/cm³ Mg-containing alloys produced by non-equilibrium routes that yield heterogeneous phase distributions.
